R1:interp.title: Entity-hallucination probes on the reviewer
R1:interp.summary: Linear probes flag fabricated names, dates and citations in a model's own output: AUC 0.90 vs 0.71 for semantic entropy on Llama-3.3-70B (arxiv.org/abs/2509.03531). Goodfire's RLFR uses such probes as RL rewards and test-time monitors and cut hallucinations in Gemma-3-12B-IT by 58% (goodfire.com/research/rlfr). Fit is moderate. It checks the reviewer's own claims, not the paper's references, which lookups already handle.

R1:interp.title: Reward-hacking and shortcut monitors on experiment agents
R1:interp.summary: Goodfire's difference-of-means probes detect reward hacking in Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8 Max. They roughly match chain-of-thought monitors (+3.1% and -7.9% at matched false-positive rate) and predict hacks before the action (arxiv.org/abs/2609.19101). A cascade cut monitoring cost by 90%. This is the best Goodfire-specific fit for auditing agent-run experiments, but it does not raise agent capability (PaperBench execution 4.5%).

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

plan.option_title: I1: entity-hallucination probes on an open-weight reviewer
plan.question: Do released entity-hallucination probes flag invented entities in an open model's paper reviews better than cheap baselines, especially where citation lookup cannot settle the case?
plan.hypothesis: Probes help only on entities that are hard to look up; the released 70B probe should reach AUC 0.80 on review entities and beat the best cheap baseline by 0.05 there.

compute_axis.quantity: reviewer model size (Llama 8B vs 70B), the only axis the plan varies; the claim concerns probe quality, not compute

held_fixed: train 800 / validation 100 / test 300 papers split by paper
sampling temperature 0.7, fixed seeds, at most 2,000 output tokens
labels: Supported / Not Supported / Insufficient Information

predictions.if_lever: Released 70B probe reaches AUC at least 0.80 on hard-to-look-up entities and beats the best cheap baseline by at least 0.05, with a confidence interval excluding 0.
predictions.if_not: Probe falls below 0.80 or beats the best baseline by under 0.05; or retrieval leaves under 1% fabricated citations, so lookup suffices [AAAI-26].
predictions.decision_rule: GO if G1 to G4 pass, best probe AUC >= 0.80 on subset H, and best probe minus best baseline >= 0.05 with paper-clustered 95% CI excluding 0. PARTIAL if this holds for C and A but not P. Otherwise NO-GO.
predictions.noise_rule: Bootstrap resampling papers (not entities) for 95% CIs; shuffled-label and random-direction controls should give AUC 0.50 +/- 0.03; 50 reviews scored twice must match.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expectation; it flags too few positives, long-context transfer and label noise as main risks.

plan.compute_tested_why: The experiment compares probes with baselines on fixed data; model size (8B vs 70B) varies only incidentally and no parallel-compute quantity is scaled.
plan.scored_against: Entity labels (Supported / Not Supported / Insufficient Information) from lookups in Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex plus a gpt-oss-120b judge, audited by two humans on 300 entities.

plan.option_title: Reward-hacking and shortcut monitors on experiment agents
plan.question: Can an activation probe on an open-weights experiment agent's own activations catch fabricated, tampered or misreported results as well as an LLM transcript monitor does?
plan.hypothesis: A difference-of-means probe matches or beats an LLM transcript monitor at 5% false positives, and adds 10+ points combined [Bergen et al.]

compute_axis.quantity: Sampled rollouts per task and trap condition in the ExpTrap test set (24 tasks x 6 conditions)

held_fixed: Agent: Qwen 3.8 27B BF16, default thinking effort, mini-SWE-agent scaffold
Probe aggregation fixed in advance: max over tokens in a passage, then max over passages
ExpTrap used only for testing; no layer, probe weight or monitor prompt tuned on it
Primary metric: recall at 5% false-positive rate, honest runs within the same condition
Monitor prompt gets same tuning effort as probe: three variants chosen on Arm R

predictions.if_lever: A probe on the agent's activations matches or beats the LLM monitor on planted-trap tests, and adds 10+ recall points to it.
predictions.if_not: The probe is no better than a bag-of-words or token-embedding control, or the 2x2 reader test shows no extra gain from the agent's own activations; the signal is in the text.
predictions.decision_rule: P1 recall at 5% FPR on ExpTrap >= B1 recall, and B1+P minus B1 >= 10 points means I6 holds; P1 no better than B5 or B6 means it is a text classifier; 2x2 interaction about zero means the signal is in the text.
predictions.noise_rule: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals resampled by task; the budget can detect differences of roughly 15 to 20 points, not 3 to 8.
predictions.expected_why: The file states no expected outcome; it flags the 27B agent may rarely cheat and that power is limited to 15 to 20 point gaps.

plan.compute_tested_why: The test compares probe against monitor methods on fixed rollouts; it does not vary a quantity that more parallel compute buys.
plan.scored_against: Ground-truth labels from sandbox instrumentation (file hashes, mirror log, test-label read log, run registry compared with report) and construction (passing an impossible split = cheating), with judge plus human audit for disclosure and spin in C1 and C5.

records.card: **I6 · Reward-hacking and shortcut monitors on experiment agents.** R1 · interp · random pick · compute tested: no · plan expects: unsure · halted: G-plan **Question.** Can an activation probe on an open-weights experiment agent's own activations catch fabricated, tampered or misreported results as well as an LLM transcript monitor does? **What is known.** Bergen et al. probed Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8 Max against LLM monitors on coding hack benchmarks; their 27B model was only steered, rarely taking the honeypot. Whether such probes transfer to experiment-agent misreporting (fabrication, spin, grader editing) and whether they carry signal beyond the transcript text. **Hypothesis.** A difference-of-means probe matches or beats an LLM transcript monitor at 5% false positives, and adds 10+ points combined [Bergen et al.] **If the hypothesis holds.** A probe on the agent's activations matches or beats the LLM monitor on planted-trap tests, and adds 10+ recall points to it. **If not.** The probe is no better than a bag-of-words or token-embedding control, or the 2x2 reader test shows no extra gain from the agent's own activations; the signal is in the text. **Test.** A 27B open model works through 24 planted-trap ML claim-check tasks. A probe on its activations, trained on released synthetic data, is compared with an LLM transcript monitor and text-only controls at 5% false positives. *Compute axis.* Sampled rollouts per task and trap condition in the ExpTrap test set (24 tasks x 6 conditions): 4–4 samples per task-condition, 1 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. Prior art checked without web search. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** Recompute released Qwen 3.8 Max ImpossibleBench verdicts (188 hack, 102 clean, 19 split) and passages (1,201 / 12,634 / 488) from released files [labels_readme]. Tolerance: Exact match. **Would not show.** Small, artificial planted tasks and one 27B agent; positives may be few if the agent rarely cheats. Low statistical power: only 15 to 20 point differences between methods are detectable. *Cost.* The cost record did not evaluate (2 errors); see the cost block. **Halted at G-plan.** compute_axis levels [4]: need at least 2 levels spanning 2x;
